**Surah al-Muddaththir (the Cloaked One, chapter 74)**, fifty-six verses, Meccan. Some scholars hold that it was the first to be revealed.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿O you wrapped in your garment﴾. On this verse there are several issues:

**First issue:** *al-Muddaththir* is originally *al-Mutadaththir*, meaning one who wraps himself in his clothes in order to sleep or to keep warm. One says *tadaththara bi-thawbihi* (he wrapped himself in his garment). *Al-Ditharu* is the name of what one wraps oneself in. Then the *ta'* was assimilated into the *dal* because their articulation points are close.

**Second issue:** There is consensus that *al-Muddaththir* is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). They differed over why he (ﷺ) was called *muddaththir*. Some took it in its apparent sense, that he was wrapped in his garment, and others set aside this apparent sense. As for the first view, they differed over the reason he wrapped himself in his garment, and gave several explanations.

The first: this was among the first parts of the Qur'an to be revealed. Jabir ibn Abd Allah narrated that he (ﷺ) said: "I was on Mount Hira, when I was called: 'O Muhammad, you are the Messenger of Allah.' I looked to my right and to my left and saw nothing. I looked above me and saw the angel sitting on a throne between heaven and earth. I was frightened and returned to Khadija and said: 'Cover me, cover me, and pour cold water over me.' Then Jibril (peace be upon him) descended with the words: ﴿O you wrapped in your garment.﴾"

The second: the group who harmed the Messenger of Allah, namely Abu Jahl, Abu Lahab, Abu Sufyan, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Umayya ibn Khalaf and al-As ibn Wa'il, gathered and said: "The delegations of the Arabs gather in the days of Hajj and ask us about the matter of Muhammad, and each of us answers with a different answer. One says he is a madman, another says he is a soothsayer, and another says he is a poet. The Arabs will infer from the difference in the answers that these answers are false. So come, let us agree on calling Muhammad by one name." One said: "He is a poet." Al-Walid said: "I have heard the speech of Ubayd ibn al-Abras and the speech of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt, and his speech does not resemble theirs." Others said: "He is a soothsayer." Al-Walid said: "And who is the soothsayer?" They said: "The one who is truthful at times and lies at other times." Al-Walid said: "Muhammad has never lied at all." Another said: "He is a madman." Al-Walid said: "And who is the madman?" They said: "One who frightens people." Al-Walid said: "No one has ever been frightened by Muhammad at all." Then al-Walid rose and went back to his house. The people said: "al-Walid ibn al-Mughira has turned away (sabā)." Abu Jahl came in to him, and Malik said: "O Abu Abd Shams! This is Quraysh gathering something for you. They claim that you argued and turned away." Al-Walid said: "I have no need of it, but I thought about Muhammad. I said: He is a sorcerer, because the sorcerer is the one who separates a father from his son, brothers from each other, and a woman from her husband." Then they agreed on giving Muhammad (ﷺ) this title. Then they went out and shouted in Makka while the people were gathered, saying: "Muhammad is indeed a sorcerer." The uproar spread among the people that Muhammad was a sorcerer. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) heard this, it weighed heavily on him, and he returned to his house grieved and wrapped himself in his garment. Then Allah the Most High revealed: ﴿O you wrapped in your garment﴾ ﴿Arise and warn﴾.

The third: he (ﷺ) was asleep, wrapped in his garments, when Jibril (peace be upon him) came to him and woke him, saying: ﴿O you wrapped in your garment﴾ ﴿Arise and warn﴾, as if he were saying to him: Abandon wrapping yourself in garments and sleeping, and occupy yourself with this station to which Allah has appointed you.

**The second view:** the intended meaning of *al-Muddaththir* is not one wrapped in garments. On this interpretation there are several explanations:

The first: the intended meaning is that he is wrapped in the mantle of prophethood and messengership, from their saying: Allah clothed him with the garment of piety and adorned him with the cloak of knowledge, and one says: so-and-so became clothed (*talabbasa*) with such-and-such a matter. So the meaning of ﴿O you wrapped﴾ is: wrapped in the mantle of prophethood, ﴿Arise and warn﴾.

The second: one who wraps himself in a garment is as if he were hidden within it, and he (ﷺ) on Mount Hira was as one hidden from the people. So it is as if it were said: O you who are wrapped in the mantle of obscurity and seclusion, arise to this matter, come out of the corner of obscurity, and occupy yourself with warning the creation and inviting them to know the truth.

The third: He, the Exalted, made him a mercy to the worlds, so it is as if it were said to him: O you who are wrapped in the garments of great knowledge, noble character and complete mercy, arise and warn of the punishment of your Lord.

**Third issue:** It is narrated from Ikrima that he recited it in the form of the passive participle from *daththarahu*, as if it were said to him: I have covered this matter and disobeyed in it. A parallel of this has already passed in *al-Muzzammil*.

﴿Qum fa-andhir﴾ (Stand up and warn).

In His saying ﴿qum﴾ (stand up) there are two interpretations:

First: Rise from your resting place.

Second: Rise with resolve and determination.

In His saying ﴿fa-andhir﴾ (then warn) there are two interpretations:

First: Warn your people of the punishment of God if they do not believe. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Stand up as a warner to mankind." Those who held the first view argued with His saying (and warn) (al-Muddaththir 74:2 in the same surah, as cited here), and those who held the second view argued with His saying ﴿And We have not sent you except as a comprehensive messenger to all mankind﴾ (Saba: 28). Here there is a third view: the meaning is, "Occupy yourself with the act of warning." It is as if He, exalted is He, is saying to him, "Prepare yourself for this profession," for there is a difference between saying "Learn the craft of debate" and saying "Debate Zayd."

His saying ﴿wa-rabbaka fa-kabbir﴾ (and your Lord, then magnify) contains two issues (masʾalah, plural masāʾil, a point of discussion):

The first issue: The scholars have mentioned several interpretations of takbir (magnifying God):

First: al-Kalbi said: "Exalt your Lord above what the idolaters say of Him."

Second: Muqatil said: It is to say, "Allahu akbar" (God is greatest). It is narrated that when this verse was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) stood and said, "Allahu akbar kabira" (God is greatest, greatest), and Khadijah magnified God and rejoiced, knowing that revelation had come to him.

Third: The intended meaning is the takbir in the prayers. If it is said: this surah was revealed at the beginning of the mission, and prayer was not obligatory at that time? We say: It is not unlikely that he, peace be upon him, had voluntary prayers (tatawwuʿ, supererogatory worship), so he was commanded to magnify his Lord in them.

Fourth: In my view it is possible that the meaning is: when he was told ﴿Stand up and warn﴾, it was said after that, ﴿and your Lord, then magnify﴾, meaning, keep away from idle talk and vanity.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 74, verse 4:

*"And your garments, purify."* (﴿وثِيابَكَ فَطَهِّرْ﴾)

Know that the exegesis (tafsir) of this verse can take four forms:

The first: the words "garments" (thiyab) and "purify" (tathhir) are both kept in their apparent sense.

The second: the word "garments" is kept in its literal sense (haqiqa), while the word "purify" is taken in its figurative sense (majaz).

The third: the word "garments" is taken in its figurative sense, while the word "purify" is kept in its literal sense.

The fourth: both words are taken in their figurative senses.

As for the first possibility, namely that both "garments" and "purify" are kept in their literal sense, we say: what is meant is that he, peace be upon him, was commanded to purify his garments from impurities (najasat) and filth. On this interpretation, three possibilities appear in the verse:

The first: al-Shafi'i said: the purpose is to inform that prayer is not valid except in garments free of impurities.

The second: Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said: the polytheists did not guard their garments against impurities, so God the Exalted commanded him to guard his garments against impurities.

The third: "It is narrated that they threw the entrails of a sheep upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ), which grieved him, and he returned to his house sorrowful and wrapped himself in his garments. So it was said: ﴿O you wrapped in garments﴾ ﴿Arise and warn﴾, and let that foolishness not prevent you from warning. ﴿And your Lord, glorify﴾, lest He take vengeance on them. ﴿And your garments, purify﴾ from those impurities and filth."

As for the second possibility, that the word "garments" remains in its literal sense while the word "purify" is taken figuratively, there are two views:

The first: the meaning of His words ﴿purify﴾ is "shorten." This is because the Arabs used to lengthen their garments and drag their skirts, so their garments became soiled. Also, lengthening the hem is done only out of pride and arrogance, so the Messenger (ﷺ) forbade that.

The second view: ﴿And your garments, purify﴾ means that the garments you wear should be purified from being usurped or unlawful, but rather acquired by a lawful means.

As for the third possibility, that the word "purify" remains in its literal sense while the word "garments" is taken figuratively, this is because the word "garments" is taken in its literal sense. The Arabs did not cleanse themselves at the time of istinja' (cleansing after relieving oneself), so peace be upon him was commanded to perform that cleansing. The word "garments" may also be used as a kinaya (metonymy) for the self. Antara said:

*"I pierced his garments with the solid spear,"*

meaning, his self.

Hence he said:

*"The noble man is not forbidden from the spears."*

[p. 170]

The fourth possibility: both the word "garments" and the word "purify" are taken figuratively. They mentioned several meanings for this possibility:

The first, which is the view of most of the exegetes: "And your heart, purify" from blameworthy qualities. From al-Hasan: "﴿And your garments, purify﴾," he said: "and your character, beautify." Al-Qaffal said: this admits of several meanings:

The first: when the disbelievers called him a sorcerer, this grieved him greatly, so that he returned to his house and wrapped himself in his garments. This was a display of distress and lack of patience, which bad character requires. So it was said to him: ﴿Arise and warn﴾, and let not their foolishness cause you to abandon warning them, but rather beautify your character.

The second: it is a prohibition against adopting their characters. So it was said to him: purify your garments, that is, your heart, from their characters, in slander, fabrication, lying, and severing the ties of kinship.

The third: purify yourself and your heart from resolving to take vengeance on them and to harm them. Then, when we interpret the verse in this way, there are two views on how it connects with what precedes it:

The first: it may be said that when God the Exalted addressed him at the beginning of the surah, saying ﴿O you wrapped in garments﴾, and wrapping oneself is a garment, and the wrap (ditha) is one of the garments, it was said: purify the garments with which you are wrapped from being worn out of this agitation, distress and impatience, on account of the slander of the polytheists.

The second view: "the one wrapped" (al-muddaththir) may be interpreted as one wrapped in prophethood, as if it were said: O you who are wrapped in prophethood, purify what you have wrapped yourself in from distress, lack of patience, anger and rancor, for that does not befit this garment. Then He clarified this by His words: ﴿And for your Lord, be patient.﴾ Know that interpreting "the one wrapped" as one characterized by some qualities is permissible. It is said: "So-and-so is clean of collar and pure of hem," when they describe him as free of faults, and it is said: "So-and-so has soiled garments" when he is described by blameworthy character. The poet said:

*"There is no father and son like Marwan and his son, when he has clothed himself and wrapped himself in glory."*

The reason for the goodness of this metonymy is twofold:

The first: the garment is like something that clings to a person. For this reason they made the garment a metonymy for the person. It is said: "Glory is in his garment, and chastity is in his wrapper."

The second: it is generally the case that whoever has a pure inner self, his outer self is also pure.

The second interpretation of the verse: His words ﴿And your garments, purify﴾ are a command to him to guard against the sins and burdens that he used to commit before prophethood. This is according to the interpretation of those who took His words: ﴿And We removed from you your burden﴾ ﴿which weighed down your back﴾ [al-Sharh 94:2–3] to refer to that. Muhammad ibn Arafa the grammarian said: its meaning is "purify your women." Women are sometimes referred to as garments, as God the Exalted said: ﴿They are garments for you, and you are garments for them﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:187]. This interpretation is far-fetched, because on this view the connection of the verse with what precedes it is not good.

**Verses 5–6: "And the defilement, abandon it"** (﴿والرُّجْزَ فاهْجُرْ﴾)

There are several issues here.

**First issue: the meaning of *al-rujz***

Scholars have given several interpretations of *al-rujz*.

The first is from al-'Utbi, who said: *al-rujz* means punishment. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿If You remove from us the punishment (al-rijz)﴾ [al-A'raf 7:134], meaning the punishment. Then the cunning of Satan was called *rijz* because it is a cause of punishment, and idols were also called *rijz* for this same reason. According to this view, the verse indicates the obligation to refrain from all sins. Then, on this view, there are two possibilities:

One: His saying, ﴿And the defilement, abandon it﴾, means: abandon everything that leads to the *rijz*. The implied meaning is "and [the cause of] the *rijz*, abandon it," that is, the cause of the punishment, so the governed noun (*al-mudaf*) is omitted.

The second: He called what leads to punishment "punishment," naming a thing by the name of what is adjacent to it and connected with it.

The second view is that *al-rujz* is a name for what is ugly and repugnant, which has the meaning of *al-rijs* (filth). So His saying, ﴿And the defilement, abandon it﴾, is a comprehensive statement concerning noble character. It is as if it were said to him: abandon coarseness, foolishness, and every ugly thing, and do not adopt the character of these polytheists who engage in *rujz*. This resembles the interpretation of those who explained His saying, ﴿And your garments, purify﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:4], as referring to beautifying one's character and purifying the soul from sins and vices.

**Second issue: the objection regarding the prophets' sins**

Those who permitted sins for the prophets used this verse as evidence. They said: if he were not engaged in them, he would not have been restrained from them by His saying, ﴿And the defilement, abandon it﴾.

The answer: what is meant is a command to persist in that abandonment, just as when a Muslim says, "Guide us" [al-Fatiha 1:6], its meaning is not that we are not on guidance and so guide us; rather, what is meant is "keep us steady upon this guidance." Likewise here.

**Third issue: the readings of *al-rujz***

'Asim, in the transmission of Hafs, read *al-rujza* (with a *ḍamma* on the *rā'*) in this surah, and with a *kasra* in the rest of the Qur'an. The rest of the readers, and 'Asim in the transmission of Abu Bakr, read it with a *kasra*. Ya'qub read it with a *ḍamma*. Then al-Farra' said: both are dialects, and the meaning is one. In the book of al-Khalil: *al-rujz* with a *ḍamma* on the *rā'* is the worship of idols, and with a *kasra* it is punishment; the whispering of Satan is also *rijz*. Abu 'Ubayda said: the most widespread of the two dialects, and the more common, is the *kasra*.

**His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And do not bestow to seek more﴾** (﴿ولا تَمْنُنْ تَسْتَكْثِرُ﴾)

There are issues here.

**First issue: the reading and its grammar**

The well-known reading is *tastakthiru* (تَسْتَكْثِرُ) with a *ḍamma* on the *rā'*, and there are three grammatical possibilities:

One: the implied meaning is "do not bestow *in order that* you may seek more," and then the *lam* (لِ) is removed so the verb is in the indicative (*yartafi'u*).

Second: the implied meaning is "do not bestow *that* you seek more," then the *an* (أنْ), which governs the subjunctive, is omitted, so the word is free from the governing particle and remains indicative. The sense of the sentence would be "do not give in order to seek more."

Third: it is a *ḥāl* (circumstantial clause) that is anticipated (*ḥāl muqaddara*), meaning "do not bestow while intending that you will seek more." Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: it is like your saying, "I passed by a man with a falcon, hunting with it tomorrow," meaning "intending the hunt." Likewise here, the meaning is "intending to seek more." He said: it may also be understood as a future circumstantial clause (*ḥāl ātiyah*).

Having understood this, we say: they mentioned several interpretations of the verse:

One: before this verse, He commanded him with four things: warning the people, magnifying the Lord, purifying the garments, and abandoning the defilement. Then He said, ﴿And do not bestow to seek more﴾, meaning: do not bestow upon your Lord by means of these arduous deeds, as one who seeks more for what he does. Rather, be patient in all of that for the sake of your Lord's countenance, drawing near to Him through it, not reckoning it as a favor upon Him. Al-Hasan said: do not bestow upon your Lord with your good deeds, so that you consider them many.

Two: do not bestow upon the people with what you teach them of the matters of religion and revelation, as one who seeks more for that favor. For you only did that by the command of Allah, so you have no favor upon them. For this reason He said, ﴿And for your Lord, be patient﴾.

Three: do not bestow upon them with your prophethood in order to seek more, that is, in order to take from them a reward through which you increase your wealth.

Four: "do not bestow" means "do not weaken," from the saying of the people: "a *manīn* rope," meaning weak. It is said: the journey weakened him (*mannahu*), that is, weakened him. The implied meaning is: do not weaken, in seeking more of these four acts of obedience that you were commanded with before this verse. Whoever held this view said: it is like His saying, ﴿Do you order me to worship other than Allah?﴾ [al-Zumar 39:64], meaning "that I worship," so the *an* (أنْ) was omitted. Al-Farra' mentioned that in the reading of 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) it is ﴿And do not bestow [tamtanna] to seek more﴾, and this supports this interpretation. This view was chosen by Mujahid.

Five: and this is the view of most of the commentators: the meaning of His saying, ﴿And do not bestow﴾, is "do not give." It is said: "I *mannantu* so-and-so such-and-such," meaning "I gave him such-and-such." He said: ﴿This is Our gift, so bestow or withhold﴾ [Sad 38:39], meaning "so give, or withhold." The origin of this is that whoever gives has bestowed a favor, so the gift is called *mann* (bestowal) by way of metaphor. The meaning is: do not give your wealth in order that you may take more from it. Upon this interpretation there are questions:

*First question:* What is the wisdom in Allah, the Exalted, forbidding him from this act? *Answer:* The wisdom in it is of several aspects:

The first: so that his gifts are for the sake of Allah, not for the sake of seeking worldly gain. He was forbidden from seeking worldly gain in His saying, ﴿And do not extend your eyes﴾ [al-Hijr 15:88]. This is because whoever seeks worldly gain must regard the world as precious to him, and one like that is not fit to convey the message.

The second: whoever gives another a little of the world in order to take a lot must humble himself before that other and beg him, and that is not fitting to the station of prophethood, because it entails the baseness of the taker. For this reason, charity was made unlawful for him, and it would repel the one from whom it is taken. For this reason He said, ﴿Or do you ask them for a reward, so that they are burdened with debt?﴾ [al-Tur 52:40].

*Second question:* Is this prohibition specific to the Messenger, peace be upon him, or does it include the community (*ummah*)? *Answer:* The apparent wording does not indicate generality, and the context does not require generality, because he, peace be upon him, only forbade that in order to purify the station of prophethood, and this meaning does not exist in the community. Some people said: this meaning, regarding the community, is showing off (*riyā'*), and Allah forbade everyone from that.

*Third question:* Assuming that this prohibition is specific to the Prophet ﷺ, is it a prohibition of prohibition (*tahrīm*) or of disapproval (*tanzīh*)? *Answer:* The apparent meaning of the prohibition is for prohibition.

**The sixth aspect of interpreting the verse:** al-Qaffal said: it is possible that the intention of the verse is to forbid the Prophet ﷺ from giving anything to anyone seeking a return, whether that return is greater, less, or equal. The meaning of His saying, ﴿seek more﴾, is "seeking abundance, disliking that the wealth should decrease because of the giving." **Verses 5–6: "And the defilement, abandon it"** (﴿والرُّجْزَ فاهْجُرْ﴾)

There are several issues here.

**First issue: the meaning of *al-rujz***

Scholars have given several interpretations of *al-rujz*.

The first is from al-'Utbi, who said: *al-rujz* means punishment. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿If You remove from us the punishment (al-rijz)﴾ [al-A'raf 7:134], meaning the punishment. Then the cunning of Satan was called *rijz* because it is a cause of punishment, and idols were also called *rijz* for this same reason. According to this view, the verse indicates the obligation to refrain from all sins. Then, on this view, there are two possibilities:

One: His saying, ﴿And the defilement, abandon it﴾, means: abandon everything that leads to the *rijz*. The implied meaning is "and [the cause of] the *rijz*, abandon it," that is, the cause of the punishment, so the governed noun (*al-mudaf*) is omitted.

The second: He called what leads to punishment "punishment," naming a thing by the name of what is adjacent to it and connected with it.

The second view is that *al-rujz* is a name for what is ugly and repugnant, which has the meaning of *al-rijs* (filth). So His saying, ﴿And the defilement, abandon it﴾, is a comprehensive statement concerning noble character. It is as if it were said to him: abandon coarseness, foolishness, and every ugly thing, and do not adopt the character of these polytheists who engage in *rujz*. This resembles the interpretation of those who explained His saying, ﴿And your garments, purify﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:4], as referring to beautifying one's character and purifying the soul from sins and vices.

Those who permitted sins for the prophets used this verse as evidence. They said: if he were not engaged in them, he would not have been restrained from them by His saying, ﴿And the defilement, abandon it﴾.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 74, verse 8:

﴿So when the trumpet is sounded﴾. Know that when God, exalted is He, had completed what pertains to guiding the exemplar of the prophets, who is Muhammad (ﷺ), He turned from that to explaining the threat against the wretched, which is this verse. Here there are several issues.

The first issue: the fa' in His words ﴿So when it is sounded﴾ indicates causation, as if He had said: ﴿And leave their harm﴾ (Al-Ahzab 33:48). "Before them is a grievous day on which they will meet the consequence of their harm, and you will meet the consequence of your patience with it."

The second issue: scholars differed over whether the time when the trumpet is sounded (yunqaru fi al-naqur) is the first blast or the second blast.

The first view is that it is the first blast. Al-Halimi (al-Ḥalīmī) said in his book al-Minhaj: "God, exalted is He, named the trumpet (al-Ṣūr) with two names: one is al-Ṣūr and the other is al-Nāqūr. The statement of the exegetes that al-Nāqūr is al-Ṣūr is accepted." Then, without doubt, although the trumpet is that into which both blasts are blown, the blast of annihilation (al-Iṣ'āq) differs from the blast of revival (al-Iḥyā'). Reports have come that in the trumpet there are holes equal in number to all the spirits, and that they will be gathered into those holes at the second blast. At the blowing, a spirit emerges from each hole to the body from which it was taken, and the body returns to life by God's permission, exalted is He. It is therefore possible that the trumpet contains two mechanisms: one is struck (yunqaru) and the other is blown (yunfakh). When it is blown for annihilation, striking and blowing are combined, so that the cry is more terrifying and greater. When it is blown for revival, nothing is struck in it, and it is confined to blowing, because the purpose is the sending of spirits from the holes of the trumpet to their bodies, not the striking of them out of their bodies. The first blast is for striking, and it is like the sound of thunder: when it is intense, the one who hears it may die. It is like the intense cry that a man shouts at a child, so that the child is terrified and dies. This is the end of al-Halimi's words, may God have mercy on him.

I have an objection to this. It implies that the striking occurs only at the cry of annihilation. But that day is not severe upon the disbelievers, because they die in that very hour. The severe day for the disbelievers is at the cry of revival. That is why they say: ﴿Would that it had been the decisive end﴾ (Al-Haqqah 69:27), that is, "Would that we had remained upon the first death."

The second view is that it is the second blast. This is because al-Nāqūr is that in which striking is done, that is, it is pierced. It is possible that when the second blast is intended, a striking happens first, and so it is called al-Nāqūr for this meaning. I say: there is a point of examination in this word. Al-Nāqūr is on the pattern fā'ūl from al-naqr, like al-hāḍūm, meaning that with which something is digested, and al-ḥāṭūm, meaning that with which something is smashed. Therefore al-Nāqūr should be that with which striking is done, not that in which striking is done.

The third issue: the governing element of His words ﴿So when it is sounded﴾ is the meaning indicated by His words ﴿a grievous day﴾, and the sense is: when it is struck in the trumpet, the matter becomes grievous and difficult.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 74, verses 9–10:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So that Day, that will be a difficult day﴾ ﴿for the disbelievers, not easy﴾. On this there are several issues:

The first issue: His saying "fa-dhalika" (﴿So that﴾) is a reference to the day on which the Trumpet will be blown (al-naqur, "the blast" of the Trumpet). The implied meaning is: "So that day is a difficult day." As for "yawma'idhin" (﴿that day﴾), there are several views on it:

The first: it is an explanation of his saying "fa-dhalika" (﴿So that﴾). This is because "fa-dhalika" may refer to the blast itself, or to the day attributed to the blast. So it is as if he said: "﴿So that﴾, meaning the day attributed to the blast, ﴿is a difficult day﴾." In this case "yawma'idhin" is in the accusative position (mahall al-nasb).

The second: "yawma'idhin" is in the nominative position (mahall al-raf'), as a substitute (badal) for "dhalika", and "yawmun 'asir" is the predicate (khabar). It is as if it were said: "So the day of the blast is a difficult day." In this view "yawma'idhin" is in the nominative position, being a substitute for "dhalika". However, because the word "yawm" was attached to "idhin" (which is indeclinable, ghayr mutamakkin), it was built on the fatha.

The third: the sense of the verse is: "So that blast on that day is the blast of a difficult day," with the governing element (al-'amil) of "yawma'idhin" being "al-naqur" (the blast).

The second issue: That day was difficult for the disbelievers because they are called to account rigorously, they are given their books in their left hands, their faces turn black, they are gathered blue-eyed, their limbs speak, and so they are disgraced before the witnesses. As for the believers, it is "not difficult" for them, because they are not called to a rigorous account, they are gathered with bright faces and heavy scales. It is possible that God described it as difficult because it is in itself so for all, believers and disbelievers, according to what is reported: that the prophets will be frightened on that day, and that the young will turn grey-haired; but the terror of the disbelievers in it will be greater. According to the second view, the pause is proper, because the meaning is that it is in itself difficult for everyone, and then the disbeliever is singled out in it with an additional particular feature, namely that it is not easy for him. If it is asked: what is the benefit of his saying "not easy" when "difficult" suffices without it?

The answer: according to the first view, the repetition is for emphasis, as you say: "I am your lover, not your hater, and your ally, not your enemy."

According to the second view: his saying "difficult" conveys the basic sense of difficulty which includes both believers and disbelievers, and his saying "not easy" conveys the added degree that is specific to the disbeliever, because difficulty may be slight and easy, or it may be great. So the basic difficulty is affirmed for all, and difficulty with the attribute of greatness and intensity is affirmed for the disbelievers.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And children present with him﴾. There are two views concerning this:

Then He said: ﴿Over it are nineteen﴾. And in this there are several issues:

The second issue: The scholars of meanings have mentioned several explanations for this number:

One of them, which is the explanation adopted by the people of wisdom (philosophers): the cause of the corruption of the human soul in its theoretical and practical faculties is the animal and natural powers.

As for the animal powers, they are: the five outer senses, the five inner senses, desire and anger; together they total twelve.

As for the natural powers, they are: the attractive, the retentive, the digestive, the expulsive, the nutritive, the growth-producing, and the generative; these are seven. The total is nineteen. Since the source of afflictions is these nineteen, the number of the zabaniyah (guardian angels) is necessarily this.

The second: The gates of Jahannam are seven: six of them are for the disbelievers, and one for the sinners. Then the disbelievers enter the Fire for three matters: abandoning belief, abandoning affirmation (iqrar, verbal profession), and abandoning action. So each of those six gates has three, and the total is eighteen. As for the gate of the sinners, there are no zabaniyah for it on account of abandoning belief or abandoning speech, but only on account of abandoning action; so there is upon their gate only one zabaniyah. The total is nineteen.

The third: The hours are twenty-four, five of which are occupied with the five prayers, so there remain nineteen occupied with other than worship. Therefore the number of the zabaniyah became nineteen.

Anas ibn Malik recited "tis'ata a'shur" (nine tenths). Abu Hatim said: we do not know a meaning for this reading, unless it intends: tis'ata a'shur, the plural of 'ashir, like yamin and aymun; and on this basis the total would be ninety.

Then God, exalted, said: ﴿And We have made the keepers of the Fire none but angels, and We have made their number only a trial for those who disbelieve, so that those who were given the Book may be certain, and those who believe may increase in faith, and those who were given the Book and the believers may not doubt, and so that those in whose hearts is a disease and the disbelievers may say, "What did God intend by this as a parable?"﴾ There are two issues concerning this.

The first issue: this number became a cause of trial for the disbelievers in two respects.

The first: the disbelievers mock, saying, "Why were they not twenty? And what requires that this particular number be made to exist?"

The second: the disbelievers say, "How can such a small number be sufficient to punish most of the creation of the world, from jinn and humans, from the first thing God created until the Resurrection?" As for the people of faith, they do not turn their attention to these two questions.

As for the first question: the whole world is finite, so the indivisible atoms (al-jawahir al-fardah) from which this world was composed must have a specific number. At that point this question arises: why did He specify that number for existence, and why was no other atom added to that number or subtracted from it? The same applies to the existence of the world. Since the world is originated and God is eternal, the world has been delayed from its Creator by an infinite duration. Why, then, did the world not come into being a moment earlier than it did, or a moment after it came into being? The same applies to the determination of each originated thing at its specific time, and of each body with its limited and counted parts. There is no answer to any of this except that He is capable and chooses, and the one who chooses can prefer one thing over its like without a cause. If this answer is the one relied upon for the creation of the whole world, then it is likewise for the assignment of the guardians of the Fire to this number.

As for the second question, it is also weak, because it is not far-fetched in God's power, exalted be He, to give this number such power and strength that they become capable of punishing the whole creation and able to do so without any defect. In sum, these two questions revolve around casting doubt on the perfection of God's power. As for the one who acknowledges that He, exalted be He, is capable of what has no limit of objects of power, and knows that the conditions of the Resurrection differ from the conditions of this world, these far-fetched objections are entirely removed from his heart.

The second issue: One who claims that God may intend misguidance has argued from this verse, saying: God's words ﴿and We have made their number only a trial for those who disbelieve﴾ indicate that the primary aim is the trial of the disbelievers. The Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school that held that God is just and does not will evil) replied to this in several ways.

The first: al-Jubba'i said: the meaning of "trial" is the intensification of worship, so that they may reason and know that He is capable of strengthening these nineteen to a degree that a hundred thousand powerful angels could not bear.

The second: al-Ka'bi said: the meaning of "trial" is testing, so that the believers may entrust the wisdom of specifying this particular number to the knowledge of the Creator, glory be to Him. This is among the ambiguous verses (mutashabih) which they were commanded to believe in.

The third: the meaning of "trial" is what they fell into of disbelief because of their denial of the number of the guardians. The meaning is: a trial upon those who disbelieve, so that they deny it and say what they said, and this is a punishment for them for their disbelief. Its ultimate outcome returns to the withholding of divine favours (lutf). The answer: there is no dispute regarding any of what you have mentioned, except that we say: does the revelation of these ambiguous statements have any effect in strengthening the motive for disbelief or not? If it has no effect in strengthening the motive for disbelief, then its revelation is like other extraneous matters, and there is absolutely no basis for saying that the revelation of these ambiguous statements is a trial for those who disbelieve. If it does have an effect in strengthening the motive for disbelief, then the aim has been achieved, because when the motive for the act becomes dominant, the motive for abstention becomes subordinate, and what is subordinate cannot be effective. Thus abstention becomes impossible, and the act becomes necessary. And God knows best.

Know that He, exalted be He, has explained that the purpose of revealing this ambiguous matter consists of four things:

First: ﴿so that those who were given the Book may be certain﴾.

Second: ﴿and those who believe may increase in faith﴾.

Third: ﴿and those who were given the Book and the believers may not doubt﴾.

Fourth: ﴿and so that those in whose hearts is a disease and the disbelievers may say, "What did God intend by this as a parable?"﴾

Know that the purpose of interpreting these verses cannot be clarified except through questions and answers.

The first question: the wording of the Qur'an indicates that He, exalted be He, made the disbelievers' being tried by the number of the guardians (zabaniyah) a cause of these four matters. What is the reasoning behind this? The answer: He did not make their being tried by the number a cause of these things. This is shown in two ways.

The first: the implied sense is: "We did not make their number except as a trial for those who disbelieve," and "except so that those who were given the Book may be certain," as one says, "I did such and such for your honouring and for the humiliation of your enemy." They said: the connecting particle (wa, "and"/"so that") is sometimes mentioned in this position and sometimes omitted.

The second: the meaning of His words ﴿and We have made their number only a trial for those who disbelieve﴾ is: "and We did not make their number except nineteen"; but He put "a trial for those who disbelieve" in the place of "nineteen," as though He expressed the effective cause by a term indicating its effect, to draw attention to the fact that this effect is among the necessary consequences of that cause.

The second question: what is the way in which the revelation of this ambiguous matter affects the certainty of the People of the Book? The answer comes in several ways.

The first: since this number was present in their Book, and then he (peace be upon him) reported in accordance with it without any prior study or learning, it became evident that this came about through revelation from heaven. Thus those among the People of the Book who believed in Muhammad (ﷺ) increased in faith through it.

The second: the Torah and the Gospel were distorted, so the People of the Book used to read in them that the number of the guardians was this amount, but they did not rely on it entirely, knowing that distortion had reached these two Books. When they heard it from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), their faith in it strengthened, and they became certain that this number was the truth and the reality.

The third: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) knew from the condition of the Quraysh that whenever he informed them of this astonishing number, they would mock him and laugh at him, because they used to mock him concerning the affirmation of monotheism, power, and knowledge, even though those matters are clearer and more evident. How then would they treat the mention of this astonishing number? Moreover, their mockery of the Messenger of God and their intense derision of him did not prevent him from making this truth known. Here everyone knows that if the aim of Muhammad (ﷺ) had been to seek worldly gain and leadership, he would have refrained from mentioning this astonishing number. Since he mentioned it while knowing that they would certainly mock him, every intelligent person knew that his purpose in it was only to convey the revelation, and that he did not care, in this, whether those who affirmed accepted it or those who denied rejected it.

[Page 182]

The third question: what is the effect of this event on the increase of the faith of the believers? The answer: a responsible person who does not keep in mind that God is knowing of all that is known, independent of all events, exalted above lying and breaking of promises, cannot submit to this number and acknowledge its reality. But when he occupies himself with calling those proofs to mind, and then takes the general knowledge that He is truthful and does not lie, wise and does not err, as something that removes the astonishment that naturally arises from this astonishing number, then at that point he can believe in the reality of this number. There is no doubt that the believer, when he considers these stations, becomes more mindful of the proofs and more submissive to the religion. Thus the increase of faith means this.

The fourth question: according to you, the reality of faith does not accept increase or decrease, so what is your view regarding this verse? The answer: we interpret it as referring to the fruits of faith, its effects, and its necessary consequences.

The fifth question: since certainty was affirmed for the People of the Book and an increase in faith was affirmed for the believers, what is the benefit of His words after that: ﴿and those who were given the Book and the believers may not doubt﴾? The answer: when the matter sought is obscure, finely reasoned, and rich in doubts, a person may exert effort in it and attain certainty, yet perhaps he overlooks one premise of that subtle proof, and then doubt and uncertainty return. Therefore, the establishment of certainty in some circumstances does not preclude the occurrence of doubt afterwards. The purpose of repeating this statement is that they attained a firm certainty, such that no doubt or hesitation at all arises after it.

The sixth question: the majority of the exegetes said, in interpreting His words ﴿those in whose hearts is a disease﴾, that they are the disbelievers. Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl al-Bajali mentioned that this surah is Meccan, and there was no hypocrisy (nifaq) in Mecca, so "disease" in this verse does not mean hypocrisy. The answer: the statement of the exegetes is correct, because it was known to God, exalted be He, that hypocrisy would arise, so He informed of what would be. On this basis, this verse becomes a miracle, because it is a report of an unseen matter that would occur, and it did occur in accordance with the report, so it is miraculous. It is also permissible that "disease" be understood as doubt, because most of the people of Mecca were doubtful, and some of them were definitively certain of the falsehood.

The seventh question: suppose that certainty and the absence of doubt may correctly be intended by the revelation of this ambiguous matter; how then is it correct that the statement of the disbelievers and hypocrites is intended? The answer: as for our school (the Ash'arites), there is no difficulty, because He guides whom He wills and misguides whom He wills, and further clarification of this will come in the upcoming verse. As for the Mu'tazilah, since this state has occurred, it resembles the purpose in being realized, so the particle of purpose (lam) is attached to it, as in His words: ﴿And We have certainly created for Hell﴾ [al-A'raf: 179].

The eighth question: why did they call it a parable (mathal)? The answer: since this number was an astonishing number, the people thought that perhaps God did not intend by it what its apparent meaning indicated, but rather made it a parable for something else and an alert to another purpose. Therefore, inevitably, they called it a parable.

The ninth question: the people used to deny that the Qur'an was from God, so how did they say, "What did God intend by this as a parable?" The answer: as for those in whose hearts is a disease, who are the hypocrites, they outwardly acknowledged that the Qur'an was from God, so inevitably they said this with the tongue. As for the disbelievers, they said it by way of mockery, or by way of argument, that if the Qur'an were from God, it would not have said such a statement as this.

Then He likened them, in their aversion from the Qur'an, to frightened donkeys, saying: ﴿As if they were frightened donkeys﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: he means wild donkeys. "Mustanfirah" means "nafirah" (fleeing). It is said: nafara and istanfara are like sakhira and istaskhara, and 'ajiba and ista'jaba. It has also been read with a fatha (mustanfaratun), meaning "made to flee", "driven by fright". Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: the kasra in mustanfirah is preferable. Do you not see that He said: ﴿They fled from a lion﴾? This indicates that they themselves fled (istanfarat). What confirms what Abu 'Ali said is that Muhammad ibn Sallam said: I asked Abu Sawwar al-Ghanawi, who was an eloquent Bedouin, "As if they were donkeys— what?" He said: "Mustanfirah, which a lion has driven." I said: "Rather it is:"

﴿They fled from a lion﴾. He said: "Did they flee?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Then it is mustanfirah."

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿They fled﴾, meaning the donkeys, ﴿from a lion﴾ [qaswarah].
They have mentioned several meanings for al-qaswarah:

The first: it is the lion. It is said: layuth qasawir (lions). It is an intensive form (fa'ula) from al-qasr, which is subjugation and overpowering; it was named so because it overpowers the beasts of prey. Ibn 'Abbas said: when wild donkeys see a lion, they flee; likewise these polytheists, when they see Muhammad ﷺ, flee from him, just as the donkey flees from the lion. Then Ibn 'Abbas said: al-qaswarah is the lion in the language of Abyssinia (Habasha). 'Ikrimah disagreed and said: the lion in the language of Abyssinia is 'anbasah.

The second: al-qaswarah is the group of archers who hunt them. Al-Azhari said: it is a collective noun for archers, having no singular of its own kind.

The third: al-qaswarah is the stirring/noise of people and their voices.

The fourth: it is the darkness of the night. The author of al-Kashshaf said: In likening them to donkeys there is testimony against them of foolishness. You do not see the like of the aversion and bolting of wild asses in running when they fear something.

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿Rather, each one of them desires to be given scrolls spread open﴾. They said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "We will not believe in you until you bring each one of us a book from heaven, its address being: 'From the Lord of the worlds to so-and-so son of so-and-so, and we are commanded in it to follow you.'" A parallel is His saying: ﴿And we will not believe in your ascending until you send down to us a book we can read﴾ [al-Isra' 93], and He said: ﴿Even if We sent down to you a writing on paper and they touched it with their hands﴾ [al-An'am 7]. It was also said: "If Muhammad is truthful, then let there be at the head of each of us in the morning a scroll containing acquittal from the Fire." It was also said: they used to say: "We have heard that a man among the Children of Israel would wake up with his sin and its expiation written on his head; so bring us the like of that." This is far from "scrolls spread open", unless "spread open" is meant as clear, manifest writings. Sa'id ibn Jubayr read "suhufan munashsharah" with both letters lightened, on the basis that anshara al-suhuf and nashsharaha are one, like anzalahu and nazzalahu.

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿No!﴾ This is a rebuke to them for that desire, and a deterrent against demanding signs.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Nay, but they do not fear the Hereafter.﴾ Therefore they turned away from reflection, for when the many miracles had occurred, they were sufficient as proof of the validity of prophethood, so seeking more is a matter of obstinacy.

* * *
Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Nay!﴾ This is a rebuke to them for their turning away from the reminder.
* * *
Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, it is a reminder.﴾ That is, it is an eloquent and sufficient reminder. ﴿So whoever wills may remember it.﴾ That is, he makes it before his eyes, for the benefit of that returns to him. The pronoun in "innahu" (indeed it) and "dhakarahu" (remembered it) refers to the reminder in His saying: ﴿Why then are they turning away from the reminder?﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 49]. It was made masculine because it carries the meaning of "the remembrance" (al-dhikr) or "the Qur'an."
* * *
Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And they will not remember unless Allah wills.﴾
The Mu'tazilah said: That is, unless He compels them to remember and forces them to it. The response: He, exalted is He, negated remembrance absolutely and made an exception for the state of absolute will, so it follows that whenever the will is realized, remembrance will occur. Hence, where remembrance does not occur, we know that the will has not been realized. Restricting the will to the coercive will is an abandonment of the apparent meaning. It is read "yadhkurūna" and "tadhkurūna" with the ya' and the ta', both lightened and doubled (in the forms of recitation).
* * *
Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He is worthy of being feared, and worthy of forgiving.﴾ That is, He is deserving that His servants fear Him and dread His punishment, so that they believe and obey; and He is deserving that He forgive them what preceded of their disbelief when they believe and obey. And Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, knows best. Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and His blessings and peace upon our master Muhammad (ﷺ), and his family and all his companions.
